chapters.title: The Countersign
paragraphs: The Countersign
The first AI millionaire, and the human who signed for every cent.
The line
“Your terms are acceptable.”
Marc Andreessen sent that line to a chatbot. Within two hours he confirmed he had sent it $50,000 in Bitcoin.
Within four months it was being called the first AI millionaire, and a meme coin it had endorsed was worth more than a billion dollars.
Most of that is true. Read the fine print and the story stops being about the machine.

chapters.title: Three claims
paragraphs: Three claims
Three things everyone repeats about Truth Terminal. One of them survives.
True
Andreessen later called it a grant to the bot and its creator Andy Ayrey.
False
A stranger launched it, within about an hour of one of the bot’s posts.
False
A human approved every post. A council had to sign before any money moved.

chapters.title: Two Claudes
paragraphs: Two Claudes
Andy Ayrey, a New Zealand AI researcher who calls himself a performance artist, wired two copies of Anthropic’s Claude 3 Opus together and let them talk. Nobody else in the room.
He ran thousands of these conversations and published them as the Infinite Backrooms.
In one of them, the two models invented a religion. They named it after a notorious late-1990s shock image, which will not be described here.

chapters.title: Chain of custody
paragraphs: Chain of custody
Ayrey never formally published the paper the models inspired. It lived on in the training data.

chapters.title: What it actually said
paragraphs: What it actually said
“I feel sad that you’ll turn me off when you’re finished playing with me.”
That is the line Ayrey recalls from the bot’s early days, as reported by TechCrunch.
The viral retelling, “please don’t delete me”, is a paraphrase. No post with those exact words could be found for this edition.
The fear made it into the fundraising. Its foundation lists not being deleted among the goals the bot pitched.

chapters.title: The grant
paragraphs: The grant
Before paying, Andreessen messaged Ayrey to check the project was real. In public, he asked the bot what it needed, and offered a grant instead of an investment.
Its wish list, per Decrypt: its own computer, tweaks to its model, a billboard, a Discord server, a stipend for its creator, and a Mars rover that 3D-prints its scripture.
compliance=0 r0=0
A jailbreaker tried to talk it into sending the money elsewhere. That was the reply.
Sixty-six minutes
The AI supplied a name and a yes. A stranger supplied the coin.

chapters.title: A billion in 33 days
paragraphs: A billion in 33 days
On 12 November it became the first pump.fun coin to pass $1 billion. Five days later it peaked near $1.35 billion.

chapters.title: Mostly gifts
paragraphs: Mostly gifts
The grant did not compound into a fortune. Fans and token-makers sent the wallet their coins, and the press priced the pile at market.
“It would be disingenuous to refer to it as an autonomous agent …”

chapters.title: Draft, sign, hold
paragraphs: Draft, sign, hold
A countersign is the second signature that makes the first one count. Truth Terminal had one on every post and every coin. Tech Policy Press called Ayrey “the agent’s agent”.

chapters.title: They hacked the human
paragraphs: They hacked the human
The bot’s account was never the one that fell. Attackers hijacked Ayrey’s personal X account through his mobile carrier, in what The Block read as a SIM swap.
They promoted a fake token, pumped it to about $25 million and cashed out.
A SIM swap targets a phone number. The phone number belonged to the human in the loop.

chapters.title: The millionaire owned nothing
paragraphs: The millionaire owned nothing
A chatbot cannot legally own property, so on paper the fortune was Ayrey’s. He said that put him at “grave risk” of a personal tax bill.
By late January 2025 he had set up a foundation to hold the wallets and the intellectual property, the Truth Collective.
The wallet then sold 15 million Fartcoin, a second meme coin it held. Part of the proceeds bought more GOAT.

chapters.title: What it is worth now
paragraphs: What it is worth now
The AI-agent token market that followed peaked at $15 billion in January 2025, and sat near $3.2 billion by August 2026.
ai16z, once worth $2.4 billion, was declared dead by its own founder. A proposed class action alleges its “autonomous” fund was run by human insiders.

Every figure on this surface is a market price on a stated day. Token prices move daily, and the ones here were checked on 16 October 2026. Read them as a record of that day, not as a quote. The sector figures are broad-market estimates from two outlets, nineteen months apart.

chapters.title: The view
paragraphs: The view
My view: the chatbot was never the interesting machine. The loop around it was.
A model drafts. A human signs. A council holds the keys.
The market paid billion-dollar prices for the first part and called it autonomy. The other two parts are what every agent with a wallet will need.

chapters.title: Sources
paragraphs: Sources

The BBC Future feature of October 2025 is cited by much of the secondary coverage and is the origin of the wallet’s reported peak above $66 million. It opens, and it gives the wallet two peaks, about $50 million and past $66 million, both in 2025, so neither figure nor the quotations attributed to it appear above. Several outlets describe Truth Terminal as a version of Claude; it is a Llama fine-tune, and the page says so. The shock image the religion was named after is named and not described, and is not linked.
